after: ## A reading routine in three passes
alt: Three passes: skim for one to two minutes (title, headings, images, captions, first and last lines) to find the text type, audience and topic; scan for the question’s key words or synonyms; then read closely around the match, checking negatives, contrast words and time words.
caption: Skim, scan, then read closely before you answer.

after: ## Worked text A: a blog post
alt: The main idea of Mira’s exchange blog is that helping with everyday jobs, especially cooking, improved her language more than sightseeing. Three supporting details back it up: learning words through need, what she could do by week three, and her advice to say yes to the boring jobs. “I pictured museums and markets” only sets up a contrast.
caption: The main idea is the point the whole text makes; details hold it up.

alt: Visual, spatial and typographic aspects each prompt a question. A strong answer names the element (the photo), describes it precisely (Mira and her hosts laughing over a chopping board) and explains its effect (the kitchen became a social place, not a chore). “There is a photo of people cooking” is weak.
caption: Name it, describe it precisely, and explain what it does to the message.

alt: A schematic community-garden poster with five annotations: the large headline at the top is read first; the photo of two smiling generations suggests the event is open to everyone; three icons match the jobs of digging, watering and harvesting; “312 kg” and a question invite readers to join; the green strip groups the practical details and suggests nature.
caption: Link each visual or spatial feature to a specific effect.

alt: For the blog and the poster: purpose (the blog entertains and advises; the poster informs and persuades), audience (people considering an exchange; local people of any age), perspective (one visitor’s view of the exchange) and attitudes (Mira values everyday contact and is relaxed about her mistakes). Word choice such as “finally trusted” is evidence of attitude.
caption: Label each one, then back it with evidence from words and visuals.

alt: Six reading question types and what earns credit: exact words for “find the word”; the right choice plus the shortest proving quotation for true or false; checking every option; rephrasing for “your own words”; name, describe and link for visuals; a label plus evidence for purpose or attitude. Example: “Mira felt confident on her first night” is false, proved by “I was nervous.”
caption: Match your answer to what the question type rewards.
